newsitem.title: PERU: Has Japan been sidelined in Peru hostage crisis?.
newsitem.headline: Has Japan been sidelined in Peru hostage crisis?.

text.p: Has Japan, which after Peru has most at stake in the Lima hostage drama, been sidelined in deciding how to deal with the crisis?
As the siege by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's residence neared the end of the fifth day, signs increasingly pointed to Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori calling all the shots.

Even the presence in Lima of Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda as an on-the-spot adviser has done little to change impressions that Tokyo, at least publicly, has decided to take a back seat to Fujimori in determing the fate of some 340 hostages.

Since arriving in Lima two days ago, Ikeda has managed only one brief meeting with Fujimori and was not told in advance of one of the key decisions so far -- to cut off water and electricity to a building which, under international law, is Japanese territory.
The lack of consultation took Ikeda by surprise, Japan's Kyodo News Agency reported.
Ikeda has spent most of his time meeting other diplomats and consoling the relatives of the scores of Japanese diplomats and Peruvian-Japanese held by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
The Japanese group is one of the biggest among the several hundred hostages held by guerrillas, many of whom are foreigners.
It took Ikeda nearly 24 hours on Saturday to get access to the latest group of freed hostages, which included three ambassadors with vital information on the situation inside the residency.
Japanese officials defended Ikeda's low profile.

"The minister is not here to be a negotiator, he is here to represent Japan and Japanese interests while its ambassador is being held," one said. "In that respect, there is no reason for him to go around pursuing discussions on strategy."

The only public sign to emerge of possible differences in the handling of the crisis was earlier this week when Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said, "Japan and Peru are far apart in ideas."

The Japanese government was quick to play down his comment, insisting that Japan, which has a record of preferring to negotiate rather than take a hard line with terrorists, fully respects Peru's handling of the matter.
The dilemma has made the generally taciturn government spokesman even more tight-lipped, resulting in mounting frustration among Japanese journalists.

Japanese officials were silent even on the key issue of whether it should be consulted before Peruvian troops storm its official property, saying only that Japan was hopeful the situation would not come to that.
Javier Perez de Cuellar, once the world's top diplomat as the Secretary-General of the United Nations, said there could be no use of force without Tokyo's approval.

"Under international conventions, that building of the embassy is inviolable," Perez de Cuellar told a local radio station on Saturday. "That means the Peruvian government has no possibility whatsoever of entering by military or police means ... without the authorization of the Japanese government."
The only other time guerrillas have taken hostages in a Japanese embassy was in February 1974, when five Palestinians took over the embassy in Kuwait, holding 12 people hostage.

Shuho Tanaka, the diplomat who led the Japanese negotiating team, arrived on the scene 11 hours after the embassy was taken over. After 50 hours Japan gave in to the guerrillas' demands and provided a plane with which they escaped.
In contrast Ikeda arrived in Lima two days after the siege began.

"...it's questionable whether Ikeda will be able to fully establish his authority at the site of the crisis, given his late arrival there," Tanaka told the Mainichi Daily News in an interview on Saturday.
